A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison: v2 contains Appendices A–F, which v3 retains and supplements with Appendix G.

before.justification: V2 reports original Craftax-classic, Craftax-full, and MinAtar experiments, including ablations and quantitative and qualitative world-model evaluations.

after.justification: V3 retains those original results and adds original MFRL and MBRL learning curves for three OpenSpiel games, evaluated in both player roles.

M1.justification: The original procedure is retained, while Section 4.7 and Appendix G introduce a substantive multiplayer variant. It bypasses NNT for symbolic observations, models both players and explicit chance actions, and expands world-model training from three prediction losses to six, adding player identity, legal-action, and chance-action targets. Policy training uses only the controlled player's observations; Tic-Tac-Toe uses an MLP without an RNN.

E1.justification: V3 adds Tic-Tac-Toe, Leduc Poker, and Bargaining from OpenSpiel, testing both player roles against uniformly random legal-action opponents. This extends coverage to multiplayer interaction with differing observability and stochasticity. Craftax-full and the four MinAtar games were already evaluated in v2.

E2.justification: Artificial Dopamine, identified as AD and attributed to Guan et al. (2024), is added to the actual MinAtar comparisons in Figures 7–9 using results supplied by its authors. The existing Craftax comparators and MinAtar MFRL/M1–M5 comparisons are retained.

E3.justification: The new OpenSpiel evaluation introduces a distinct design: separate player-role experiments against random opponents, privileged observations for world-model training, a budget of 100k actions across both players, and imagination training without warmup. Existing experiment settings are retained. The added MinAtar comparison in Figure 9 explicitly juxtaposes AD at 5M steps with the paper's agents at 1M, rather than using equal budgets.

E4.justification: The component, patch-size, quantization, RNN, and warmup ablations are retained, as are annealing, reconstruction-error, symbol-accuracy, and rollout case analyses in Sections 4.3–4.4 and Appendices C–D. The new OpenSpiel results are benchmark comparisons, without additional ablations or diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: Both versions specify means and standard errors over 10 seeds. V3 also reports its OpenSpiel comparisons over 10 seeds, continuing the existing reporting practice. No increased run count for retained experiments or new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedure is reported.

E6.justification: Figure 10 adds multiplayer learning curves showing especially strong early MBRL advantages. Figure 9 adds AD's 5M-step rewards of 21.05, 27.78, 57.68, and 140.36 for Asterix, Breakout, Freeway, and SpaceInvaders, respectively. The paper's own per-game MinAtar values remain unchanged, while its normalized summary changes from 2.41 to 2.43. Existing Craftax results are retained.

T1.justification: Appendix G newly defines joint player-observation/action sequences and player/chance action domains, asserting that action identity determines the player. This is a limited addition to the formal specification; existing NNT, BTF, PPO, and VQ-VAE mathematics is unchanged. The written Player 2 and chance-action ranges overlap at their boundary, despite the asserted distinctness.

C1.justification: The three central method contributions and principal Craftax performance claims remain. The rewritten abstract and revised conclusion broaden the explicit generality claim to include three two-player games and highlight preliminary results beyond Craftax-classic. Their mentions of Craftax-full and MinAtar partly promote evidence already present in v2.

C2.justification: V3 interprets the multiplayer results as evidence that useful symbolic world models can be learned from tens of thousands of interactions, with no warmup needed in these simple games. It explicitly assumes random opponents and fully visible world-model training observations. Existing interpretations of tokenization, compounding errors, and patch-related limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendix G and Tables 9–10 add implementation information specific to OpenSpiel: observation and action cardinalities, reward encoding, action indexing, prediction targets, conditional RNN use, and hyperparameters including 2,000 world-model and imagination-policy updates. Existing implementation descriptions, hardware and timing information, and code references are retained.

R1.justification: V3 adds references to Guan et al. for Artificial Dopamine, Lanctot et al. for OpenSpiel, Lewis et al. for Bargaining, and Southey et al. for Leduc Poker. These support the added comparisons and domains; the existing related-work discussion and positioning of the original method remain unchanged.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten to explain the three improvements before summarizing benchmark evidence. V3 adds Section 4.7 and Appendix G, revises the MinAtar discussion and conclusion, and clarifies a few references to policy updates in imagination. Most existing prose and section organization are retained.

P2.justification: V3 adds the six-panel OpenSpiel Figure 10 and parameter Tables 9–10. Figures 7–8 gain AD curves and legend entries, and Figure 9 gains an AD column and budget labels, with some resizing. Existing appendix figures are retained and renumbered; the overall visual format remains stable.

improvement.justification: V3 provides a useful external MinAtar comparison and documented evidence extending the framework to multiplayer games. Its corrected normalized reward of 2.43 also agrees with the unchanged Figure 9 values. These gains are limited: multiplayer tests use random opponents and privileged world-model observations, omit NNT and warmup, and introduce an action-indexing ambiguity in Appendix G. The core Craftax evidence remains unchanged.
